stem: An 18-year-old man wakes unable to lift his legs after a carbohydrate-rich dinner the night before. Strength is normal between attacks. Serum potassium during an attack is 2.4 mEq/L, and thyroid function is normal. His father has had similar episodes.
oneliner: 18M + flaccid leg weakness on waking after carb-rich dinner + K 2.4 during attack + normal thyroid + normal between attacks + father similarly affected → which gene?
ask: Mutation of which gene is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: X-linked recessive disease cannot pass from **father to son**, and dystrophy gives **progressive** weakness, not attacks with normal strength between them
whyNot.C: RYR1 defects cause **malignant hyperthermia** after anesthetics or central core disease, not weakness after a **carbohydrate meal** with **low potassium**
whyNot.D: Chloride channel loss causes **myotonia** (stiffness that eases with repeated use), with **normal potassium**
whyNot.E: Myotonic dystrophy gives **myotonia, cataracts and progressive weakness** with normal potassium, not **flaccid attacks with K 2.4**

why: **Episodic flaccid weakness** after carbohydrate, with **low potassium during attacks** and **normal strength between**, in a patient with an **affected father**, is **hypokalemic periodic paralysis**. It is an **autosomal dominant** channelopathy, usually in the **L-type calcium channel gene CACNA1S**, less often SCN4A.

idea.rule: Periodic paralysis is a muscle ion-channel disease inherited as autosomal dominant, with attacks triggered by carbohydrate or rest after exercise.
also: SCN4A (sodium channel) causes the less common form
Insulin and carbohydrate push potassium into cells, triggering attacks
Treatment during an attack is oral potassium
Hyperkalemic form: SCN4A, attacks after potassium intake

stem: A newborn girl has short proximal limbs, a large head with frontal bossing and a flattened nasal bridge. Both parents have normal stature and no family member is affected. The mother is 29 years old and the father is 52.
oneliner: Newborn F + short proximal limbs + large head, frontal bossing + both parents normal height + mother 29, father 52 → how did the mutation arise?
ask: Which of the following best explains how this mutation arose?

options.A: Advanced maternal age causing meiotic nondisjunction
options.C: Uniparental disomy of the chromosome carrying FGFR3
options.D: Inheritance from an unaffected carrier mother
options.E: New FGFR3 mutation in paternal sperm

whyNot.A: Maternal age raises **trisomy** risk, but her mother is only **29** and this is a single-gene skeletal dysplasia
whyNot.B: Diabetes raises risk of caudal regression and cardiac defects; **nothing in the stem** mentions maternal diabetes
whyNot.C: Disomy gives disease through **imprinting or recessive** genes (Prader-Willi, Angelman), not a dominant growth-plate disorder
whyNot.D: A carrier mother implies **recessive** inheritance; this is **dominant**, and unaffected parents would not be silent carriers

answer: A new (de novo) FGFR3 mutation arising in the father's germline, linked to advanced paternal age
why: Short **proximal limbs** with **frontal bossing** and **normal-height parents** is **achondroplasia**. Most cases are **sporadic**: a **new gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation** in **paternal sperm**, more frequent with a **father of advanced age** (here 52).

idea.rule: Most achondroplasia is a new autosomal dominant FGFR3 mutation from the father, and risk rises with paternal age.
also: Advanced paternal age also raises risk of Marfan syndrome, Apert syndrome, and schizophrenia
An affected parent passes the gene to each child with a 50% chance

stem: A 5-year-old boy has frequent falls and uses his hands to push up from the floor to stand. His calves are enlarged and firm. Creatine kinase is very high, and a muscle biopsy shows no dystrophin on immunostaining.
oneliner: 5M + falls + pushes up with hands to stand + enlarged firm calves + very high CK + no dystrophin on stain → which mutation type?
ask: Which type of mutation most likely explains his disease?

options.A: Frameshift deletion of the dystrophin gene
options.B: In-frame deletion of the dystrophin gene
options.C: Expanded CTG repeat in the 3' untranslated region
options.D: Missense mutation in a sarcoglycan gene
options.E: Homozygous deletion of the SMN1 gene

whyNot.B: An **in-frame** deletion leaves a **shortened but partly working** dystrophin (Becker); his stain shows **no dystrophin** and onset is at 5
whyNot.C: A CTG expansion causes **myotonic dystrophy**: myotonia and cataracts, with dystrophin present; his stain shows **no dystrophin**
whyNot.D: Sarcoglycan mutations give **limb-girdle dystrophy**, not an X-linked pattern with **absent dystrophin**
whyNot.E: SMN1 deletion causes **spinal muscular atrophy**: hypotonia with tongue fasciculations and normal or mildly raised CK, not **calf enlargement with absent dystrophin**

answer: Frameshift deletion in the dystrophin gene (Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
why: Early-onset **Gowers sign**, **calf pseudohypertrophy**, very high **CK** and **absent dystrophin** is **Duchenne**. A **frameshift** deletion in this X-linked gene abolishes the protein, whereas an **in-frame** deletion leaves a shorter, partly working protein and causes the milder, later-onset **Becker** disease.

idea.rule: Frameshift deletions give Duchenne (no dystrophin); in-frame deletions give Becker (reduced or truncated dystrophin).
also: Reading-frame rule applies to deletions of one or more exons
X-linked recessive: carrier mothers are usually unaffected but can show mild weakness or cardiomyopathy
Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a common cause of death in both forms
